children: Campari spent decades teaching Americans to love the Italian tradition of bitter aperitifs at sunset. Now, it is finally giving U.S. drinkers something sweeter to sip on.

The company on Tuesday kicked off a promotional campaign for Sarti Rosa, a relatively recent entry to its portfolio of liquors designed to be turned into spritzes. Sarti and its accompanying cocktail, the Sarti Spritz, diverge from the citrus-heavy, herbal tastes of Aperol and the company's namesake Campari with a tropical taste of mango, passion fruit and blood orange.
Campari hopes the brand will interest drinkers who have rejected its existing offerings, claiming another chunk of land in the growing but increasingly competitive spritz category.

"If consumers consider Aperol still too bitter, Sarti is definitely an easier gateway to the spritz category," said Andrea Neri, managing director of Campari's House of Aperitivi. "It skews a bit younger," Neri added, noting that its hot pink color encourages social media posting as much as Aperol's orange hue.

Campari in turn plans to market Sarti as the young, fun, rebellious sibling of its portfolio. The company aims to drum up intrigue this week by placing oversize pink luggage trunks across New York City before sailing a pink branded boat around Manhattan. It is planning a party in the Meatpacking District, and will partner with the "Adults" actor Owen Thiele to host a branded live taping of a podcast episode. More promotional activities will take place in San Diego later this month.
But much of Sarti's marketing was set in motion before Campari's U.S. operation spent a single dollar on advertising.

The company over the past few years has been introducing Sarti to markets across Europe, starting in 2022 in Germany, expanding across the Alps into Italy, Austria and Switzerland and finally making a debut in France and the U.K. earlier this year. The influx of American tourists to Europe, particularly during the spritz-happy summer months, sparked a flurry of word-of-mouth recommendations, Instagram posts and TikTok videos from those who had tried the drink abroad and wanted to drink it again in the States.

North American bartenders on Reddit asked for substitution and shipping suggestions in bids to re-create the spritz they tried in Europe, while local publications later wrote guides to finding the cocktail in their area. In Campari's most recent earnings report, Sarti was named as the primary driver of an 8.8% organic sales lift in its "other aperitifs" category, which excludes Aperol and Campari.

"I finally found somebody who would ship a bottle to me but the shipping cost as much as the bottle," the American author Eli Rallo said in a TikTok post recounting her quest to get hold of Sarti. Rallo said she was "desperado" for the aperitif-"almost desperate enough to fly to London just to have one."

Campari has been drip-feeding Sarti to U.S. bars, restaurants and retailers since June in what Neri, the aperitifs boss, called a scarcity approach to drive demand. When Manhattan restaurant Uva started serving the aperitif in July, it posted to Instagram: "The spritz everyone's trying to get their hands on just landed."
Many of the first stockists have limited consumers to a one- or two-bottle purchase, Campari Chief Executive Simon Hunt told analysts on an earnings call in July.
Sarti's rollout comes as Campari faces greater competition in the spritz category that it spent millions of dollars developing in the U.S.

Beverage industry columnists and analysts in recent months have questioned whether the collective Aperol appetite is waning in favor of the Hugo Spritz, an elderflower-based cocktail usually made with Bacardi's St-Germain liqueur. St-Germain's year-over-year sales growth in the U.S. has outpaced Aperol's for the past two summers, according to an analysis of NielsenIQ data by the investment bank Jefferies.

But sales of Aperol still tower over those of St-Germain. Aperol is the 29th bestselling spirit brand worldwide by volume, selling almost 10 million nine-liter cases in 2025, according to trade publication the Spirits Business. St-Germain doesn't appear in the top 150.

Campari contends that a growing, wider spritz category is good for the company, adding that the introduction of Sarti in Europe has broadened the company's reach without cannibalizing its other brands.
